# 1 Maccabees Chapter 6 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, 1 Maccabees 6 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/1MA_006_page_001.jpg

---

1. King Antiochus was moving through the upper provinces when he heard that in Persia there was a city called Elymais, renowned for its wealth in silver and gold.
2. Its temple was very rich, with golden shields, breastplates, and weapons left there by Alexander son of Philip, the Macedonian king who first ruled over the Greeks.
3. He came to try to take the city and plunder it, but he could not succeed, because the people of the city learned of his plan
4. and rose up against him in battle. He fled, and departed in great distress, to return to Babylon.
5. While he was still in Persia, a messenger came with news that the armies sent into Judah had been defeated:
6. that Lysias had advanced with a strong force but had been driven back before the Judeans; that the Judeans had grown strong in arms and resources, with a large store of plunder taken from the defeated armies;
7. that they had demolished the abomination he had erected on the altar in Jerusalem, and had surrounded the sanctuary with high walls as before, and had also fortified Beth-zur, one of his cities.
8. When the king heard these words, he was astonished and deeply shaken. He lay down on his bed and fell into a sickness born of grief, because things had not turned out as he had planned.
9. He remained there many days, for deep grief kept returning to him, and he realized he was dying.
10. He summoned all his Friends and said to them: "Sleep has fled from my eyes, and my heart is heavy with worry.
11. I said to myself: 'What great trouble has come to me! Into what a flood of misery have I sunk — I who was kind and beloved in my power!'
12. But now I remember the wrongs I did in Jerusalem — how I seized all the gold and silver vessels that were in it and sent to destroy the inhabitants of Judah for no good reason.
13. I know that it is because of this that these miseries have overtaken me; and here I am, dying in bitter grief in a foreign land."
14. Then he summoned Philip, one of his Friends, and appointed him over his whole kingdom.
15. He gave him his crown, his robe, and his signet ring, with instructions to raise his son Antiochus and to install him as king.
16. King Antiochus died there in the one hundred and forty-ninth year.
17. When Lysias learned that the king was dead, he installed the king's young son Antiochus in his place — the boy he had raised — and called him Eupator.
18. Meanwhile the garrison of the citadel was blockading Israel around the sanctuary, constantly seeking to harm them and to strengthen the Gentile cause.
19. Judas resolved to destroy them, and called all the people together to besiege them.
20. They gathered and laid siege in the one hundred and fiftieth year; he built siege-towers and war machines against them.
21. But some of those inside the citadel escaped, joined by certain renegades of Israel,
22. and went to the king and said: "How long will you fail to act and bring justice for our cause?
23. We were willing to serve your father, to live by his decrees and follow his orders.
24. For this our own countrymen have been besieging us; and they have put to death every one of us they could lay hands on, and plundered our estates.
25. Not only against us have they stretched out their hand, but against all our territory.
26. Even now they are encamped against the citadel in Jerusalem to seize it; and they have fortified the sanctuary and Beth-zur.
27. If you do not act against them quickly, they will go even further, and you will not be able to stop them."
28. When the king heard this, he was enraged. He assembled all his Friends, the commanders of his infantry, and the commanders of his cavalry.
29. Mercenary forces came to him from other kingdoms and from the islands of the sea.
30. The total of his forces was one hundred thousand infantry, twenty thousand cavalry, and thirty-two elephants trained for battle.
31. They came through Idumea and encamped before Beth-zur. They attacked it over many days and built siege engines; but the garrison sallied out and burned them and fought courageously.
32. Judas withdrew from the citadel and moved to Beth-zechariah, opposite the king's camp.
33. The king rose early and moved his army swiftly along the road to Beth-zechariah. The forces took up battle formation and sounded the trumpets.
34. They showed the elephants the blood of grapes and mulberries to rouse them for battle.
35. The animals were distributed among the phalanx units. Each elephant was accompanied by a thousand men wearing coats of mail and wearing bronze helmets, and five hundred chosen horsemen were assigned to each beast.
36. These were ready wherever the beast was; wherever it went, they went with it and never left its side.
37. On the elephants were wooden towers of strength, one fastened on each beast with a special harness. On each tower were four fighting men who fought from it, and also an Indian mahout.
38. The remaining cavalry was stationed on either side, at the two flanks of the army, to harass the enemy and to provide cover within the infantry units.
39. As the sun shone on the golden and bronze shields, the mountains gleamed with them and blazed like torches of fire.
40. Part of the king's army spread out over the upper hillsides, and part over the lower ground; they advanced confidently and in good order.
41. All who heard the noise of their multitude, the tramp of the companies, and the clash of weapons were shaken — it was a very great and powerful army.
42. Judas and his army advanced to engage, and six hundred men from the king's army fell.
43. Eleazar, called Avaran, noticed that one of the elephants was equipped with royal armor and was the tallest of them all; he assumed the king was riding on it,
44. and gave himself up to save his people and to win himself an undying name.
45. He ran boldly toward it through the midst of the phalanx, cutting down men on right and left, and they parted before him on both sides.
46. He got in under the elephant and stabbed it from below and killed it; the elephant crashed down on him, and he died there.
47. Seeing the might of the royal army and the ferocity of its assault, the Judeans pulled back from them.
48. The king's forces advanced against them toward Jerusalem; the king encamped in Judea and before Mount Zion.
49. He made peace terms with the people of Beth-zur; they surrendered the city, because they had no food to endure a prolonged siege, for it was a sabbatical year for the land.
50. The king took Beth-zur and stationed a garrison there to hold it.
51. He then encamped against the sanctuary for many days, setting up there machines of war, catapults, fire-throwers, stone-hurlers, scorpions to shoot arrows, and slings.
52. The defenders also built machines to counter the king's machines; the siege continued for many days.
53. But there were no provisions in the storerooms, because it was the seventh year, and the refugees who had fled to Judea from the Gentiles had consumed whatever was left of the stores.
54. Only a few men remained in the sanctuary; the rest had scattered to their homes, for hunger had overcome them.
55. Then Lysias learned that Philip — whom King Antiochus while still alive had designated to raise his son Antiochus as king —
56. had returned from Persia and Media with the army that had accompanied the king, and was now trying to seize control of the government.
57. In his urgency to leave, he said to the king, the commanders, and the troops: "We are growing weaker every day; our provisions are scarce; the place we are besieging is strong; and the affairs of the kingdom demand our attention.
58. Let us therefore offer terms to these men, make peace with them and with their whole nation,
59. and allow them to live according to their own customs as before; for it was our abolishing their customs that provoked them to anger and to do all these things."
60. The proposal pleased the king and the commanders, and he sent them an offer of peace, which they accepted.
61. The king and the commanders swore oaths to them on all these terms; the garrison came out of the stronghold.
62. The king then entered Mount Zion; when he saw how strong the position was, he broke the oath he had sworn and ordered the surrounding wall to be demolished.
63. He then departed in haste and returned to Antioch, where he found Philip already in control of the city. He fought against him and took the city by force.
